title: The Queen Goes In
sum: On the third day of the fast Esther dresses as queen and stands in the inner court, where coming unbidden means death (4:11). The king holds out his gold scepter, and she touches it. He offers her anything, up to half the kingdom. She asks only that the king and Haman come to a feast she has made. At the feast the king asks again, and again she asks only for a second feast, tomorrow.

Haman leaves happy, until he sees Mordecai in the king's gate, who will not rise for him. At home he boasts to his friends and his wife Zeresh of his wealth, his sons and his honors, and then admits that none of it is worth anything while Mordecai sits there. Zeresh and his friends advise him to build a pole fifty cubits high and ask the king in the morning to hang Mordecai on it. He likes the plan, and the pole is built that night.
readings: Read as a court story

Chapter 5 is a lesson in patience. Esther has the king's open promise, but she uses it to set a scene she controls: a private feast, then another, with the king's curiosity growing and his promise repeated each time. Haman, by contrast, cannot wait a single day. The wise courtier and the fool are drawn side by side, a pattern known from Proverbs and from the Joseph story (Talmon).
Read as the turning of the plot

The chapter ends with everything set for disaster. Haman has a pole, a plan for the morning, and the queen's favor, as he thinks. The reader knows what Haman does not: the queen is a Jew. The real turn waits for the night that follows (6:1).
Read with the Greek

In the Greek Esther, the scene at the throne is the book's emotional peak. Addition D shows Esther fainting before an angry king, and God changing his heart. The Hebrew tells the same moment in two calm sentences and never names God. The two forms of the book show two ways of telling the same faith.

views.H: Traditional readers take the scene as it stands: a real queen at the court of Xerxes, risking her life on the third day of a fast and using wisdom to approach her request. The scepter, the throne room facing the doorway and the feasts all fit what is known of the Persian court.
views.C: Critical scholars read the chapter as skilled storytelling: two feasts to build suspense, the boasting villain, and a pole of absurd height. Many think the double feast and the delay are devices to give the night of chapter 6 room to happen. The Greek Additions are seen as later expansions that make the religious meaning explicit.
views.A: Susa's palace and its columned hall (apadana) have been excavated, and reliefs from Persepolis show a king enthroned with a long scepter receiving a visitor. Herodotus describes strict rules of access to the king and Persian pride in many sons, both of which the chapter assumes.
views.J: The rabbis asked why Esther invited Haman and offered many answers (Bavli Megillah 15b). They read "she put on royalty" as "she was clothed with the holy spirit" (Bavli Megillah 14b), and later tradition found God's name hidden in the first letters of 5:4. Esther's entry on the third day is joined to other third-day rescues (Genesis Rabbah 56:1).
views.X: Christian readers have seen in Esther's going in a picture of courage and of intercession: she risks her life to plead for her people. Some saw a type of Christ, who goes before the King on behalf of others, or of the church approaching God's throne with confidence (Hebrews 4:16). The "third day" has suggested the resurrection to many.

deep.b:
Why does Esther wait? The narrator does not say, and the gap invites the reader in. Three answers are common. Nerve. She starts to speak (5:7) and stops; she may simply have lost her courage. Strategy. A second invitation commits the king more deeply: he has now promised twice, the second time in front of Haman, and she has framed her request as something he asked of her (5:8). Providence. The delay allows the sleepless night of 6:1, so that by the time Esther speaks Mordecai has already been honored and Haman humbled.

The three answers can stand together. The book often lets human planning and unexplained timing work side by side, and leaves the reader to decide what lies behind the timing.

The Septuagint replaces 5:1–2 with a long scene, called Addition D (Rahlfs 5:1a–f, 2a–b). After her prayer (Addition C), Esther takes off her mourning clothes and dresses "in her glory." She goes in with two maids, radiant on the outside and frozen with fear inside. The king looks up "burning with glory" in fierce anger, and she faints. Then "God changed the spirit of the king to gentleness" (Greek 5:1e). He leaps up, holds her, and tells her that the law is only for ordinary people. She says she saw him "like an angel of God," and faints again.

The Hebrew has none of this. The Greek makes the scene more dramatic and makes God the cause of the king's change of heart. The Alpha Text has a similar scene. The Additions are read as Scripture by Catholic and Orthodox Christians and not by Jews or Protestants; the variants on 5:1 and 5:2 summarize them.

echoes: 4:11; 4:16; Genesis 22:4; Genesis 43:31; Genesis 45:1; Exodus 19:16; Hosea 6:2; Mark 6:23; Proverbs 16:18; Deuteronomy 21:22–23

settings.what: The king's offer and Esther's two invitations
settings.to: Each other, first in the throne room, then at the wine feast with Haman present
settings.when: The third day of the fast of 4:16, after the king held out his scepter
settings.why: The king's words ("up to half the kingdom") are a royal promise of favor. Esther's answers are meant to bring the king and Haman together in a place she controls, and to build the king's commitment before she makes her real request. Knowing that she is a Jew under sentence of death, hiding that fact in front of the man who wrote the decree, changes every polite word into a risk.
settings.readers: For Jews living as a minority under Persian and later Greek kings, the scene showed how a Jew in a foreign court might use the rules of that court with patience and skill, rather than open defiance, to save the community.
views: Hesitation
Esther's nerve fails at 5:7 and she puts off the request.
Strategy
The delay is deliberate: it deepens the king's promise and sets up Haman (Fox, Bush).

settings.to: His friends and his wife Zeresh, gathered at his house in Susa
settings.when: The evening after Esther's first feast, after Mordecai refused to rise for him
settings.why: Haman lists his wealth, sons and honors to hear them praised, and then confesses his one grievance. The speech shows the reader his pride and his weakness: all his success is spoiled by one man's refusal to honor him.
settings.readers: For the first readers, Haman's boast drew the enemy of the Jews as a vain and small man, more to be scorned than feared, whose pride is the very thing that will undo him.

settings.to: Haman, at his house
settings.when: The same night, after his boast
settings.why: They offer a quick fix for Haman's misery: kill Mordecai the next morning, then enjoy the queen's feast. The plan assumes the king will agree at once, as he did to Haman's decree (3:8–11). The pole's height is meant for all of Susa to see.
settings.readers: The first readers would hear the irony: the advice that seems to promise Haman joy builds the pole on which he will die (7:9–10). Zeresh will speak again, very differently, in 6:13.

title: The Sleepless Night
sum: That night the king cannot sleep. He has the royal records read to him and hears how Mordecai once saved his life from two plotting eunuchs (2:21–23). He asks what reward Mordecai received and is told: nothing. At that moment Haman arrives in the outer court, come early to ask for Mordecai's death. Before he can speak, the king asks him, "What is to be done for the man the king takes pleasure in honoring?" Sure that the king means himself, Haman describes a royal parade: the king's clothes, the king's horse with a royal crown, a noble leading it and calling out praise.

The king tells Haman to do it all for Mordecai the Jew. Haman leads Mordecai through the city square, shouting his honor, then hurries home in mourning. His wise men and Zeresh now tell him that if Mordecai is a Jew, he will surely fall before him. While they are still speaking, the king's eunuchs arrive to take Haman to Esther's second feast.
readings: Read as the turning point

Many scholars find in 6:1 the hinge of the whole book. Before it, Haman rises and the Jews are condemned; after it, every step reverses (Berg; Levenson). The chapter is built on irony: Haman writes the script of his rival's triumph and then must perform it.
Read as providence

Nothing in the chapter is a miracle: a king cannot sleep, a servant reads a certain page, a man arrives early. Jewish and Christian readers have long seen in such timing the hidden hand of God, and the Greek says plainly that "the Lord took the sleep away from the king." The Hebrew leaves the reader to draw that conclusion.
Read as comedy

Fox and others note how funny the chapter is: Haman's thought in his heart, the king's innocent question, Haman's growing list of honors for himself, and his public role as Mordecai's herald. Purim's tradition of laughter and parody grows from scenes like this one.

views.H: A real night in the life of Xerxes, recorded because it changed the fate of the Jews. Traditional readers see God's providence in the timing, though the Hebrew does not say so.
views.C: Critical scholars see a carefully built reversal, perhaps the book's center, with motifs from the Joseph story (royal clothes, a horse, a herald). The delay between Mordecai's deed (2:23) and his reward is a storyteller's device that makes the timing perfect.
views.A: Persian kings were known for recording and rewarding their benefactors. Herodotus says Xerxes' scribes noted men who served well (8.85; 8.90), and a letter of Xerxes in Thucydides promises that a benefactor's service is "recorded forever" (1.129). That makes the failure to reward Mordecai a striking lapse.
views.J: The Talmud reads "the king" as the King of the universe, whose sleep "fled" when his people were in danger (Bavli Megillah 15b). Esther Rabbah 10:1 sets this night beside two psalms, one saying that Israel's guardian never sleeps (Psalm 121:4) and one calling on the Lord to wake (Psalm 44:23). The Talmud also tells how Haman's daughter, mistaking the man on foot for Mordecai, emptied a chamber pot on her father's head (Bavli Megillah 16a). Zeresh's warning is read as the confession of Israel's enemies that they cannot finally prevail.
views.X: Christian commentators from the Reformers on have used 6:1 as a classic text on providence: God governs the smallest events, such as a king's insomnia, to keep his promises. The reversal of Haman and Mordecai has been compared to the song of Hannah and of Mary: God brings down the proud and lifts up the humble (1 Samuel 2:7–8; Luke 1:52).

deep.b:
The honor Haman designs for himself matches Joseph's honor in Egypt. Pharaoh had Joseph clothed in fine linen, gave him a gold chain and his signet ring, "had him ride in his second chariot, and they shouted ahead of him, 'Abrek!'" (Genesis 41:42–43). Mordecai is dressed in the king's clothes and led through the city on the king's horse with a herald calling out (6:11); later he receives the signet ring (8:2) and becomes second to the king (10:3).

Other echoes join the two stories: a Jew rises in a foreign court, a hidden identity is revealed at the right moment, and the family is saved. Many scholars think the author of Esther wrote with the Joseph story in mind, and some use the parallels to argue that Esther is a deliberately crafted court story. Others answer that real Persian court customs would produce the same scenes.

echoes: 2:21–23; Genesis 41:42–43; 1 Kings 1:33; 2 Samuel 15:30; Psalm 121:4; Exodus 17:8–16; Joshua 2:9–11; 1 Samuel 2:7–8; Luke 1:52

settings.what: The king's question about Mordecai's reward
settings.to: His young men, the servants attending him that night
settings.when: During the sleepless night, after the account of 2:21–23 was read
settings.why: The king wants to know whether a debt of honor has been paid. A Persian king's honor depended on rewarding those who served him, so the answer "Not a thing" calls for action at once.
settings.readers: For the first readers, the scene showed that a Jew's loyal service to a foreign king, unnoticed for years, was not lost. Faithfulness to the empire and faithfulness to one's people could go together.

settings.what: The king's question to Haman, and Haman's answer
settings.to: Haman, newly arrived in the court; then the king
settings.when: Early in the morning after the sleepless night, before Haman could ask to hang Mordecai
settings.why: The king asks for advice on how to honor someone, without naming him. Haman, assuming he is the one, designs the honor he wants most: to be seen in the king's own clothes, on the king's own horse, with a royal crown. His answer reveals his ambition to share the trappings of the throne, which is why many readers think the king notices.
settings.readers: The first readers would enjoy the irony and learn its lesson: the proud man writes the script of his own humiliation. For a community that had heard Haman's decree read against it, the scene turned fear into laughter.
views: Innocent question
The king simply wants advice and does not know of the quarrel (most readers).
Testing Haman
Some suggest the king notices Haman's request for royal symbols and grows wary of him, which prepares for 7:8.

settings.what: The herald's cry in the city square
settings.to: The crowds in the open square of Susa
settings.when: The same morning, as Mordecai rides through the city
settings.why: A public proclamation of royal honor: everyone in the city is to see whom the king delights to honor. That Haman must shout it makes the reversal public too.
settings.readers: Jews hearing the Megillah read at Purim have always enjoyed this moment; it is one of the scenes acted out in Purim plays.

settings.what: The king's order: do it for Mordecai
settings.to: Haman
settings.when: Immediately after Haman's answer
settings.why: The king turns Haman's advice into an order and names Mordecai "the Jew" who sits in the king's gate. Haman must carry out every word himself.
settings.readers: For Jews living under foreign rule, the king's words "Mordecai the Jew" were striking: the very people Haman had condemned is named with honor in the king's mouth.

settings.what: Zeresh and the wise men foresee Haman's fall
settings.by: Haman's wise men and his wife Zeresh
settings.to: Haman, at home after the parade
settings.when: Between the parade and Esther's second feast
settings.why: Those who advised the pole now warn Haman that his fall has begun and cannot be stopped if Mordecai is a Jew. Their words act as a prophecy inside the story; they do not offer any way out.
settings.readers: For the book's first readers, scattered and vulnerable, hearing their enemies' own household say that the Jews' enemies cannot prevail was a word of hope. The Greek makes the reason explicit: "the living God is with him."

title: The Pole Haman Built
sum: At the second feast the king asks Esther a third time for her request. Now she speaks: she asks for her life and her people's lives, for they have been sold to be annihilated, killed and destroyed. If they had only been sold as slaves, she says, she would have kept quiet. The king demands to know who has dared to do this. Esther points: "The adversary, the enemy, is this evil man, Haman!"

The king storms out into the palace garden. Haman stays to beg the queen for his life and falls on her couch just as the king returns. The king takes it as an assault on the queen. Haman's face is covered. The eunuch Harbona mentions the fifty-cubit pole Haman built for Mordecai, "the man whose words did the king good." The king says, "Hang him on it." Haman dies on his own pole, and the king's rage cools.
readings: Read as justice

The chapter shows the moral pattern of the book: the plotter is caught in his own plot. Haman is hanged on the pole he built for Mordecai, an example of the biblical teaching that the one who digs a pit falls into it (Psalm 7:15–16; Proverbs 26:27).
Read as court politics

Esther wins by speaking carefully. She never accuses the king, though he sealed the decree; she makes Haman the enemy of the king as well as of her people. Haman is condemned for a crime he did not commit (assaulting the queen), while his real crime is never judged. Some readers find this troubling; others see a realistic picture of how power works at court.
Read as Esther's coming out
Here Esther finally says who she is. The orphan who hid her people (2:10) stands with them, risking the same death. For Jews in the diaspora, this has been one of the book's central lessons.

views.H: Traditional readers take the events as history: Esther revealed her identity, and the king executed Haman for his treachery. They see God's justice working through human choices.
views.C: Critical scholars note the neat symmetry of the chapter and its fairy-tale justice, and read it as the climax of a crafted plot. Some point out that the king's charge is unfounded and that the narrator leaves Haman's real guilt to the reader.
views.A: Greek writers report that Persian kings guarded their women closely and that approaching them was a grave offense (Plutarch, Artaxerxes 27). Impalement and public display of the executed were Persian punishments (Herodotus 3.159; the Behistun inscription).
views.J: The Talmud says an angel pushed Haman onto Esther's couch (Bavli Megillah 16a). Harbona is honored in the Purim song Shoshanat Ya'akov: "and also Harbona be remembered for good." The final letters of 7:7 were read as another hidden form of God's name.
views.X: Christian readers have seen in Haman's fall a picture of God's judgment on those who persecute his people, and in Esther's plea a model of intercession. The pole also became a point of conflict: a Roman law of AD 408 (Theodosian Code 16.8.18) forbade Jews to burn a figure of Haman on a cross-like frame at Purim, because Christians took the custom as mockery of the cross.

deep.b:
Haman's death on his own pole is the clearest of the book's reversals, and Mordecai's letter later sums it up: Haman's plot came back "on his own head" (9:25). The idea runs through the Bible. A psalm of David says that the one who digs a pit falls into the hole he has made, and that his violence comes down on his own head (Psalm 7:15–16). A proverb says that whoever digs a pit will fall into it, and a stone will roll back on the one who rolls it (Proverbs 26:27). Daniel's accusers are thrown to the lions they intended for him (Daniel 6:24). (Psalms, Proverbs and Daniel are described here, not quoted, because they are not yet translated on this site.)

In Esther, though, no voice from heaven sends the stone back. The reversal is carried out by a queen's courage, a eunuch's timely remark and a king's temper. Readers differ on whether that is a picture of God's justice working through ordinary people, or a story in which justice simply happens.

echoes: 3:8–11; 4:7; Deuteronomy 28:68; 1 Samuel 20:7; 1 Samuel 20:33; Psalm 7:15–16; Proverbs 26:27; Daniel 6:24; 2:1

settings.what: Esther's plea for her life and her people
settings.by: Queen Esther, answering the king's question
settings.to: King Ahasuerus, with Haman present, at the second wine feast
settings.when: The second day of feasting, after Haman's public humiliation that morning
settings.why: Esther asks for her own life and her people's, reveals that she belongs to the people condemned, and then names Haman as the enemy. Every phrase is chosen: "sold" recalls Haman's money (3:9); she says she would have kept quiet over mere slavery; she leaves the king's own role unspoken. Her aim is to turn the king's anger on Haman, not on his own decree.
settings.readers: For Jews who could pass unnoticed among their neighbors, and were sometimes tempted to, Esther's plea was the moment when a Jew who could have hidden chose to stand with her people. It made the book a call to solidarity and courage, and a model of wise speech before rulers.
views: Courage
Most readers stress her bravery in revealing herself.
Tact
Others stress her careful rhetoric, especially in sparing the king (Fox, Berlin).

settings.what: The king's demand: who has done this?
settings.to: Queen Esther, with Haman sitting at the table
settings.when: At once, after Esther says she and her people have been sold to be destroyed
settings.why: The king asks who has dared to do it, as if he did not know of the decree he sealed (3:10–11). The question gives Esther the opening to name Haman, and lets the king act as judge rather than as the one who signed the order.
settings.readers: The first readers would notice what the king forgets. A ruler who signs away a people's lives without asking who they are was a real danger for a minority, and the scene laughs at that danger while it shows it.

settings.to: Haman (and the servants present)
settings.when: As the king comes back from the garden and finds Haman on the queen's couch
settings.why: The king's question is an accusation, almost certainly unfair, that gives him a reason to condemn Haman without condemning the decree he himself sealed. The servants understand it as a death sentence and cover Haman's face.
settings.readers: The first readers would see the irony: Haman, who falsely accused a whole people (3:8), is condemned on a false charge. The book does not dwell on whether that is just.

settings.by: Harbona, one of the king's eunuchs
settings.to: King Ahasuerus
settings.when: Immediately after Haman's face is covered
settings.why: Harbona supplies the last piece the king needs: Haman built a pole for Mordecai, the man who saved the king's life. The remark turns Haman's crime into treachery against the king's benefactor and suggests the means of execution.
settings.readers: For the first readers, Harbona showed that help can come from unexpected people inside the empire. Jewish communities still bless his memory at Purim.

settings.to: Harbona and the servants present, who carry it out (7:10)
settings.when: Immediately after Harbona's remark, at the second feast
settings.why: A royal death sentence, given in two Hebrew words (teluhu alav) with no trial. It punishes Haman with the very pole he had prepared for Mordecai.
settings.readers: For the first readers, the sentence was the book's plainest picture of a plot falling on its maker, a pattern they knew from their own Scriptures (Psalm 7:15–16).

title: A Second Decree
sum: Haman is dead, but his decree still stands: on the 13th of Adar the Jews may be killed and plundered. The king gives Haman's house to Esther and his signet ring to Mordecai. Esther falls at the king's feet in tears and begs him to reverse Haman's letters. The king answers that a document written in his name and sealed with his ring cannot be turned back, but Esther and Mordecai may write whatever they think good, in the king's name.

On the 23rd of Sivan, Mordecai dictates a new letter to every province, in every script and language, and to the Jews in their own. It gives the Jews in every city the right to gather and defend themselves on the 13th of Adar against any force that attacks them. Fast horses carry it across the empire. Mordecai leaves the palace in royal clothes, the city of Susa cheers, and the Jews have light and joy. Many people of the land "make themselves Jews," for dread of the Jews has fallen on them.
readings: Read as law

The chapter is about how to undo an unjust law in a system that cannot repeal it. The answer is a counter-law: Mordecai's letter copies Haman's almost word for word (compare 3:12–14 with 8:9–14), but gives the Jews the right to defend themselves. Two decrees stand side by side, and the empire's officials must choose which to follow.
Read as reversal

Almost everything in the chapter mirrors chapter 3: the ring changes hands, scribes are summoned again, couriers ride again, and a city in turmoil (3:15) now cheers (8:15). The mourning of 4:3 becomes the light and joy of 8:16–17.
Read with the Greek

The Greek adds the text of the king's second letter (Addition E), in which the king calls Haman a Macedonian traitor and praises the Jews as children of the Most High God. Where the Hebrew is quiet about God and about the king's conscience, the Greek makes both speak.

views.H: Traditional readers take the counter-decree as a real Persian edict, explaining it by the irrevocable law of the Medes and Persians (1:19; Daniel 6:8). They see Mordecai's rise and the conversions of 8:17 as fruits of God's care.
views.C: Critical scholars note that no Persian source mentions irrevocable laws and see the rule as a plot device that makes the final battle necessary. Many read the close copying of chapter 3 as deliberate literary design.
views.A: The royal post and its fast horses are well attested (Herodotus 8.98), and Persian decrees were sent out in local languages; Aramaic was the empire's common written language. The rare words for the horses in 8:10 are Persian loanwords. Persepolis tablets record travelers carrying sealed royal documents.
views.J: 8:16, "For the Jews there was light and joy, gladness and honor," is recited at the close of every Sabbath in the Havdalah service. The Talmud reads its four nouns as Torah, festivals, circumcision and tefillin (Bavli Megillah 16b). Those who "made themselves Jews" (8:17) are discussed as converts, sincere or not.
views.X: Christian readers have seen in the counter-decree a picture of the gospel: a sentence of death that cannot simply be erased is met by a new word from the king that brings life. Others have used the chapter to reflect on Christians' duty to work within unjust systems for the protection of the vulnerable.

deep.b:
Mordecai's letter (8:9–14) repeats Haman's (3:12–14) almost phrase by phrase: the scribes, the satraps, governors and officials, every province in its own script and every people in its own language, the king's name and seal, the runners, the 13th of Adar, and the triple verbs "annihilate, kill and destroy." Even "little children and women" and "their property ... taken as plunder" are copied (on the debated meaning, see the note on 8:11).

Two things change. The letter goes "to the Jews" as well as about them, in their own script and language; and it grants defense, not attack: the Jews may act against "every army of any people or province that comes against them." The result is a strange legal situation. From Sivan to Adar both letters are in force. Anyone who attacks the Jews may do so under the first decree, and the Jews may resist under the second. The officials of the empire back the Jews, the text says, because dread of Mordecai has fallen on them (9:3).

After 8:12 the Septuagint prints the text of the king's new letter (Rahlfs 8:12a–x). It is written in a polished Greek style and was almost certainly composed in Greek. The king, called Artaxerxes, warns against officials who abuse royal kindness. He calls Haman a Macedonian, a foreigner "with no Persian blood," who plotted to kill Mordecai and Esther and to hand the empire to the Macedonians. He declares the Jews no criminals but people who live by the most just laws, "children of the Most High, the most mighty living God." Haman, he says, has been hanged at the gates of Susa with his household. The letter orders that the Jews may keep their own laws, that they be helped on the 13th of Adar, and that the day be kept as a festival.

The addition pairs with Addition B, Haman's letter after 3:13. In both, the Greek gives the reader the documents the Hebrew only describes. Unlike Additions A, C, D and F, which may go back to a Hebrew or Aramaic original, B and E were composed in Greek (Moore; Martin). In the Greek, Haman is said to have been crucified, the word the Greek also uses at 7:9.

echoes: 3:10–15; 1:19; Daniel 6:8; Daniel 6:15; Genesis 41:42; Exodus 15:16; Joshua 2:9; Deuteronomy 2:25; Isaiah 56:3–6; Zechariah 8:23; Proverbs 11:10

settings.to: King Ahasuerus, in the palace; she comes again, apparently unbidden, and he again holds out the scepter
settings.when: The day of Haman's death, or soon after, with Haman's decree still in force
settings.why: Esther asks the king to reverse Haman's letters, piling up four polite conditions and calling the letters "the plot of Haman" rather than the king's decree. Her questions ("How could I stand to watch...?") appeal to the king's love for her. She asks not for herself, now safe, but for "the Jews" and "my kin."
settings.readers: For the first readers, Esther showed that the rescue of one Jew at court was not enough: she had to go back and plead for all. Her tears and persistence modeled advocacy for a whole people.

settings.to: Queen Esther and Mordecai the Jew
settings.when: In answer to Esther's plea
settings.why: The king points to what he has already done (Haman's house given, Haman hanged) and hands Esther and Mordecai the power to write a new decree in his name, sealed with his ring. He explains that a sealed royal document cannot be turned back, and he does not take responsibility for the first one.
settings.readers: For Jews living under foreign kings, the reply showed the limits of royal favor: the king would help, but only by letting them help themselves.

settings.by: Mordecai, writing in the name of King Ahasuerus, with the king's seal
settings.to: The Jews in every city, and the satraps, governors and officials of all 127 provinces from India to Cush, each province in its own writing and the Jews in theirs; a copy was also to be shown openly to all the peoples (8:13), including any who planned to attack
settings.when: Written on the 23rd of Sivan, about seventy days after Haman's decree (3:12), to take effect on the 13th of Adar
settings.why: The letter cannot cancel Haman's decree, so it creates a second law: the Jews may gather and defend themselves against any army that comes against them on that day. Published as law in every province and shown to all the peoples, it warned would-be attackers that the Jews could now fight back lawfully, and it told the Jews to be ready for the day (8:13). Its wording copies Haman's letter to show that the same royal power now protects the people it had condemned. The phrase about "little children and women" is debated (see the note on 8:11).
settings.readers: For a minority that had heard a royal decree read against it, the decree showed that the law of a foreign empire, which had threatened them, could be turned to protect them. It also gave legal standing to the fighting of chapter 9, presenting it as lawful defense under the king's authority.
views: Lawful self-defense
The decree permits defense only against attackers (most traditional readers; Gordis on 8:11).
Mirror-image wording
The decree grants the Jews the same powers Haman had claimed, families and plunder included (Fox, Moore); the narrative then shows the Jews using less than they were allowed.

title: The Day Turned Upside Down
sum: On the 13th of Adar, the day Haman's lot had chosen, the enemies of the Jews hoped to rule over them, "but it was turned upside down." The Jews gather in their cities and strike those who seek to harm them, while the empire's officials back them out of fear of Mordecai. In the fortress at Susa they kill five hundred men and Haman's ten sons. At Esther's request the king allows a second day in Susa, and Haman's sons are hung on the pole; three hundred more are killed in Susa on the 14th, and seventy-five thousand in the provinces. Three times the text says they kept their hands off the plunder.

Then come rest and feasting: the provinces rest on the 14th and Susa on the 15th, which is why villagers and city dwellers keep different days. Mordecai writes to all the Jews to keep both days every year with feasting, sending portions of food to one another and gifts to the poor. The days are named Purim after Haman's lot (pur). The Jews take the festival on themselves and their descendants and all who join them. Esther writes a second letter with full authority, and her word confirms the rules of Purim.
readings: Read as self-defense

The Jews act on the day set for their destruction, under a royal decree, against those who come to harm them; they take no plunder. On this reading the chapter records a people's lawful defense in a world where the first decree could not be withdrawn (Baldwin, Bush, Berlin).
Read as a story of reversal

Many literary and critical readers see the chapter as the last of the book's reversals, told with large numbers and symmetrical days, to give hope to a vulnerable people rather than to report a battle. Its emphasis falls less on the killing than on the rest and the feast that follow (Fox, Levenson).
Read as a festival charter

The second half of the chapter (9:20–32) reads like a legal text: it fixes dates, customs and authority for Purim. Many scholars think it was added to bind a festival already being kept; others see it as the goal toward which the whole story moves.

views.H: Traditional Jewish and Christian readers take the fighting as historical self-defense under an irrevocable decree, and the founding of Purim as the act of Mordecai and Esther. The refusal to take plunder shows that the Jews fought for their lives, not for gain.
views.C: Critical scholars generally doubt that such a massacre took place, since no outside source mentions it, and see the numbers as part of a story of reversal. Many think 9:20–32 is a later appendix and debate whether Purim came from the story or the story from an existing festival (see the deep section).
views.A: Purim's name comes from Akkadian puru, "lot," a word attested on an inscribed Assyrian die (Hallo). Babylonian month names (Adar) and Persian administrative terms fit the setting. No Persian or Greek source records the events of the 13th and 14th of Adar.
views.J: This chapter founds the Purim laws: the reading of the Megillah, the feast, mishloach manot and gifts to the poor (9:19, 22), and the two dates, with walled cities keeping the 15th (Mishnah Megillah 1:1). The names of Haman's sons are written in a column and read in one breath (Bavli Megillah 16b). The Talmud reads 9:27 to say the Jews accepted the Torah anew in Esther's day (Bavli Shabbat 88a).
views.X: Christians have been divided over this chapter. Some, like Luther, found its spirit troubling; others defended it as just self-defense and a picture of God's deliverance. Many Christian readers set it beside Jesus' teaching on loving enemies (Matthew 5:44) while noting that the Jews here act in defense under law, not in private revenge.

deep.b:
Few chapters in the Bible trouble modern readers more. Three main approaches are taken, and each is held by serious readers.

Self-defense under an unchangeable law. Haman's decree could not be revoked (8:8). On the 13th of Adar, anyone who wished could attack the Jews legally. Mordecai's decree allowed the Jews to resist "every army of any people or province that comes against them" (8:11), and they acted against "anyone who was looking to do them harm" (9:2). They took no plunder (9:10, 15, 16), and only men are counted among the dead (9:6, 15). This is the view of most traditional Jewish and many Christian commentators (Baldwin, Bush, Berlin, Jobes).

Revenge. Others read 9:5, "They treated those who hated them however they wanted," and Esther's request for a second day (9:13) as signs of vengeance beyond defense. Paton wrote that the book has not one noble character, and Luther wished it did not exist, though his stated complaint was that Esther and 2 Maccabees "Judaize too much" (Levenson, Berlin), a theological objection more than a moral one. Jewish readers have faced the question too, most sharply after a Jewish settler killed 29 Muslim worshipers in Hebron on Purim in 1994; Elliott Horowitz has traced how the chapter's memory was used, and resisted, in Jewish history.

A story of reversal. Many literary and critical scholars think the chapter is not a battle report but the last turn of a story built on reversals: the destruction planned for the Jews falls on their enemies, in the same words (Fox, Levenson, Clines). The large, round numbers and the stress on rest and feasting (9:16–19) point the reader to relief, not slaughter. On this view the book was written for a powerless minority who imagined, and celebrated, being saved from those who hated them.

The text itself makes several things clear: the fighting was on the day set by Haman's lot, it was authorized by the king, and the Jews refused the plunder the decree allowed. Whether it was just, and how far it went, the narrator leaves the reader to judge.

As the book tells it. Purim celebrates the Jews' rescue from Haman, who cast the pur, the lot, to choose the day of their destruction (3:7; 9:24). The 14th and 15th of Adar are kept as days of rest after the fighting on the 13th (and 14th in Susa). Mordecai and Esther wrote to make the feast binding (9:20–32). This is the view of Jewish tradition and of most traditional Christians.

Critical theories. In the late 1800s scholars noted that Mordecai's name is built on that of Marduk, chief god of Babylon, and that Esther sounds like Ishtar, Babylon's great goddess. Heinrich Zimmern (1891) argued that Purim came from the Babylonian New Year festival, when the gods fixed the fates of the year. Peter Jensen (1892) read the story as a Jewish form of a Babylonian myth, with Haman and Vashti matching the Elamite gods Humban and Mashti. Paul de Lagarde (1887) had proposed the Persian festival of the dead, Farvardigan, and Theodor Gaster (1950) argued that Purim adapted the Persian New Year festival.

Assessment. The name links are real, but they prove less than once thought. Jews in exile often bore names built on foreign gods' names (Daniel 1:7), and "Marduka" is a common name in Persian-period records. No Babylonian or Persian myth with this plot has been found, and Purim's customs do not match the New Year rites. Most scholars now think Purim began as a festival of the eastern Jewish diaspora, whose name came from pur, "lot," and whose founding story is the book of Esther, whatever older popular customs it may have absorbed (Moore, Fox, Levenson). The earliest outside witness is 2 Maccabees 15:36, which calls the 14th of Adar "the day of Mordecai."

deep.h: The Greek and the Alpha Text in chapter 9
deep.b:
The Septuagint differs from the Hebrew at many points in this chapter. It lacks the words "it was turned upside down" in 9:1, saying only that the king's letters arrived. It lacks 9:5. It says "and they plundered" in 9:10 but "they plundered nothing" in 9:15 and 9:16, and it has fifteen thousand dead in the provinces, not seventy-five thousand (9:16). In 9:13 Esther asks for a second day "so as to hang the ten sons of Haman," which makes the hanging the purpose of the request. It adds that city dwellers keep the 15th (9:19), says Mordecai wrote these things "in a book" (9:20), calls Haman "the Macedonian" and gives "a decree and a lot" for Pur (9:24), and makes Haman the one who went to the king in 9:25. It names the festival Phrourai (9:26) and Esther's father Aminadab (9:29).

The Greek of 9:29–32 is shorter. It has no "second" letter (9:29), lacks 9:30 with its "words of peace and truth," and has no "fasts and their cries for help" in 9:31, so the custom of the Fast of Esther has no basis in this form of the text. In 9:32 Esther's word is "written for a memorial" rather than in a book.

The shorter Greek Alpha Text differs still more. In it Esther asks that the Jews be allowed "to destroy and plunder" whomever they want, the opposite of the Hebrew's refusal of plunder, and it counts 700 dead in Susa and 70,100 in the kingdom (NETS). It names the eunuch of 7:9 Agathas, says at 8:17 that many of the Jews were circumcised, and lacks most of 9:20–32, keeping only a brief notice of Mordecai's letter and the feast. Clines argued that the Alpha Text preserves a form of the story that once ended at 8:17, and that the Purim regulations were added later; others think the Alpha Text shortened a longer text (Fox, Jobes, De Troyer). The variants on these verses give the readings.

deep.title: "It was the people who took from the spoil"
deep.b: Claude's reading. When Samuel confronted Saul over the spoil of Amalek, Saul blamed the people: "It was the people who took from the spoil some sheep and cattle" (1 Samuel 15:21). In Esther the refusal of the plunder is told three times, and each time the subject is not a leader but "the Jews" as a body: in Susa on the 13th (9:10), in Susa on the 14th (9:15), and in all the provinces (9:16). The threefold report may be answering Saul's excuse: this time the whole people, in every place and on every day, does what Saul's people did not. The contrast between Saul's plunder and the Jews' refusal is well known in scholarship (Levenson, Berlin) and in Jewish tradition; what is added here is only the link to Saul's blaming of "the people" in 1 Samuel 15:21 and the reading of the three reports as covering the whole people.

echoes: 3:7; 3:13; 8:11; 1 Samuel 15:3; 1 Samuel 15:9; 1 Samuel 15:19; 1 Samuel 15:21; Deuteronomy 25:17–19; Exodus 17:8–16; 2 Samuel 5:10; Nehemiah 8:10–12; Zechariah 8:19; Isaiah 56:3–6; Jeremiah 31:13; 2 Maccabees 15:36

settings.what: The king's question and Esther's request for a second day
settings.to: Each other, at the palace in Susa
settings.when: On that day, the 13th of Adar, after the count of the dead in Susa reached the king
settings.why: The king reports the numbers and asks, for the fourth time in the book (5:3; 5:6; 7:2; 9:12), what more Esther wants. Esther asks that the Jews of Susa be allowed to act under the decree for one more day, and that the bodies of Haman's sons be hung up for all to see. The text gives no reason. She may have known that enemies remained in the capital; she may have wanted Haman's house publicly disgraced; the request also explains why Susa kept a different day.
settings.readers: For the first readers, this exchange explained the second day of Purim kept in Susa and later in walled cities (9:18–19). It has also become the most debated moment of Esther's character.
views: Prudence
Enemies remained in Susa, and a second day ended the danger (Baldwin, Jobes, Bush).
Vindictiveness
Esther goes beyond defense (Paton and other older critics).
Etiology
The scene exists to explain the 15th of Adar in Susa (Clines, Fox).
The Greek forms
The Septuagint gives the hanging of Haman's sons as the purpose of the second day; the Alpha Text has Esther ask leave to destroy and plunder (NETS).

settings.what: The king's law for a second day in Susa
settings.to: The Jews of Susa and the people of the city, where it was given out as law
settings.when: The 13th of Adar, for the 14th, one more day only
settings.why: The first counter-decree covered only the 13th (8:12). This law extends it in the capital for one day, so that the Jews of Susa may act again against those who come against them, and it orders the public display of Haman's sons. It answered the danger that enemies remained in Susa, or, read as an explanation of custom, why Susa kept its feast a day later than the provinces (9:18).
settings.readers: For the first readers, this short law explained why the Jews of Susa, and later of walled cities, keep Purim on the 15th of Adar (9:18–19). It is the root of Shushan Purim.

settings.to: All the Jews in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, near and far
settings.when: After the fighting and the first celebrations, to fix the custom for every year
settings.why: The letters turn a spontaneous celebration into a yearly obligation. They set two days, the 14th and 15th of Adar, for feasting, sending portions of food and giving gifts to the poor, and they give the reason: rest from enemies and sorrow turned to joy. The retelling of Haman's plot (9:24–25) supplies the meaning of the name Purim. The letters bind the Jews, their descendants and those who join them, in every generation and place.
settings.readers: For Jewish communities scattered from Persia to Egypt, who had no Temple feast of their own for this rescue, these letters were the charter of the festival: a feast not commanded by Moses, set by Jewish leaders in exile, and accepted by the people. They taught a scattered people to remember their rescue together, in every city, on the same days, and to include the poor and the newcomer.
views: Part of the story
Mordecai's letter is the goal toward which the story moves (Fox, Levenson).
Later appendix
9:20–32 was added to an earlier story to authorize an existing festival (Paton, Clines).

settings.by: Queen Esther, with Mordecai the Jew
settings.to: All the Jews in the 127 provinces of the kingdom of Ahasuerus
settings.when: After Mordecai's first letter, to confirm it
settings.why: Esther uses "all her authority" as queen to make the Purim rules binding, and Mordecai sends the letters, with "words of peace and truth," to all the provinces (9:30). The letter places Purim alongside the fasts the Jews had already taken on, and her word fixes the rules in writing.
settings.readers: For the first readers, Esther's letter gave the festival a second, royal authority, and made a woman the one whose word confirmed a binding religious custom for all Israel. Jews keeping Purim still trace their customs, including the Fast of Esther, to these verses.
views: A second letter
Esther's letter confirms Mordecai's (9:20) with her own authority.
Editorial addition
Some think the word "second" or the whole section was added later (Moore). The Septuagint has no "second," lacks 9:30, and has no fasts in 9:31.

title: Mordecai the Great
sum: The book ends with a short notice in the style of the royal records. King Ahasuerus puts a tax on the land and on the islands of the sea. His mighty deeds, and the full account of how he raised Mordecai to greatness, are written in the records of the kings of Media and Persia. Mordecai the Jew is second only to the king, great among the Jews, loved by his many brothers, working for his people's good and speaking peace to all his descendants.

There is no word of God, no return to Jerusalem, and no prayer. The Hebrew book closes with a Jew in high office in a foreign empire, caring for his people. The Greek continues with Addition F, in which Mordecai says, "These things have come from God," and with a note about the Greek translation's arrival in Egypt.
readings: Read as a royal epilogue
The closing verses use the formula of Kings ("are they not written...?") and set Mordecai beside the king in official history. They give the story the weight of a public record.
Read as a model for the diaspora

The book ends not with a return home but with a good life lived abroad: a Jew serving the empire and his people at once. Many scholars see this as the book's message to Jews scattered among the nations (Levenson; Berlin).
Read with the Greek ending

In the Greek, Mordecai's dream from the beginning of the book is explained, and the two lots become God's lots, one for his people and one for the nations. The Greek closes the frame that the Hebrew leaves open.

views.H: Traditional readers take 10:2 as a pointer to real Persian records and see Mordecai's greatness as the reward of faithfulness, like Joseph's and Daniel's.
views.C: Critical scholars see a conventional ending modeled on Kings and on the Joseph story. Some think 10:1–3 was added with 9:20–32. No Persian chronicle of the kind named here survives, and Mordecai's office is unknown outside the Bible.
views.A: Herodotus describes Persian tribute from the provinces (3.89–97). After 479 BC Persia lost most of the Aegean islands, which bears on how literally "the islands of the sea" should be read. Tablets name officials called Marduka, though whether one is Mordecai is debated (Yamauchi; Clines).
views.J: The Talmud notes that 10:3 says Mordecai was accepted by "the crowd of his brothers," not all of them, and reads this as a sign that some sages were displeased that he left Torah study for public office (Bavli Megillah 16b). The verse is read as praise of a leader who sought his people's good.
views.X: Christian readers have compared Mordecai to Joseph and Daniel, faithful servants of God at a foreign court, and some to Christ, exalted after humiliation to the right hand of the king (Philippians 2:9). The Greek ending, part of Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, makes the book's faith in God explicit.

deep.b:
The Septuagint closes with Addition F (Rahlfs 10:3a–k) and a colophon (10:3l). In Addition F, Mordecai says, "These things have come from God," and explains the dream of Addition A, which opens the Greek book: the little spring that became a river is Esther; the two dragons are Haman and Mordecai; the nations gathered to wipe out the name of the Jews. God made two lots, one for his people and one for the nations, and when the hour came he remembered his people and vindicated his inheritance. The 14th and 15th of Adar are to be kept with joy before God forever.

The colophon says that "in the fourth year of the reign of Ptolemy and Cleopatra," Dositheus, who said he was a priest and a Levite, and his son Ptolemy brought this "letter of Phrourai" to Egypt, saying it was genuine and had been translated by Lysimachus son of Ptolemy, a man of Jerusalem. Bickerman dated it to 78/77 BC; others prefer 114/113 BC or 49/48 BC. It shows the Greek Esther being sent from Jerusalem to promote Purim among the Jews of Egypt. On any of these dates, the Greek book was meant to carry the festival to a new community.

The Hebrew book ends without naming God, without the Temple or Jerusalem, and without a call to return. Jewish readers have long found God hidden in its events, and the Talmud links Esther's name to God's words "I will keep my face hidden" (Deuteronomy 31:18; Bavli Chullin 139b). Christian readers have seen the same hidden providence. Critical readers have explained the silence in different ways: as the book's character as a festival scroll read in noisy celebration, as reverence for the name, or as a deliberately secular court tale. Whatever the reason, the Hebrew leaves the reader with a question that the Greek answers outright.

echoes: 1 Kings 11:41; 1 Kings 15:31; Genesis 41:40–43; Daniel 5:29; Daniel 6:2–3; 2 Chronicles 28:7; Deuteronomy 31:18; 2 Samuel 5:10

settings.to: The land and the islands of the sea, that is, the whole empire to its farthest coasts
settings.when: After the events of Purim, at an unstated time
settings.why: A royal levy, reported in one line in the style of official records. It shows the king's power reaching across land and sea, and it may contrast with the release he gave the provinces at Esther's crowning (2:18).
settings.readers: For the first readers, the notice set the story back into ordinary imperial life: the king still taxes, the empire goes on, and a Jew stands second to the king within it (10:3).
